extracted.intended_audience: postgraduate research students preparing a thesis / research degree candidates
extracted.subtask_description: Guidelines for preparing, formatting and writing a scientific-style postgraduate thesis, covering appendices, headings, figures/tables, numbers, grammar, style and punctuation. Intended to ensure clarity, consistency and conformity with university requirements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appendices — appropriate content
rubrics_metrics.description: Appendices may include tables that are too detailed for presentation in text; large groups of illustrations; technical notes on methodology; forms used in collecting materials/data; copies of relevant documents; illustrative materials such as figures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: All Appendices should go at the end of your thesis (back matter). Place materials of different categories in separate Appendices. When there are numerous Appendices, each is given a number or a letter (Appendix 1 or Appendix A). Provide a clear title for each section. Check supervisor/school preference.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appendices — page numbering
rubrics_metrics.description: The page numbers used in the Appendices are separate from those of the main thesis and are to be presented as: A-1, A-2, A-3, etc.

rubrics_metrics.name: Headings and subheadings — formatting and capitalization
rubrics_metrics.description: Main headings (i.e. of chapters/main sections) should be in bold type. Subheadings and sub-subheadings should not be in bold type.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Full capitalization is used for main headings (e.g. 2.0 Materials and Methods). For subheadings and sub-subheadings, capitalize the first word only (e.g. 2.1 Volume data sets). For headings of figures and tables, use capitals for the first word only (e.g. Figure 1 Incidence of hospital-acquired infections). The table number and title is placed above a table. The figure number and title is placed below a figure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Font size and style
rubrics_metrics.description: Use an appropriate, readable font (in general, a font such as Times New Roman 12 should be used).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Refer to the University Guidelines for Research Degree Programmes for exact rules of font size, style and format and check supervisor/school requirements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Spacing
rubrics_metrics.description: Present your work in either 1.5 or double spacing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Verify which spacing your supervisor recommends at your initial meeting and check university guidelines.

rubrics_metrics.name: Illustrations — clear purpose and self-contained
rubrics_metrics.description: Before you use a figure or table, make sure that it has a clear purpose. Each figure or table should be self-contained: readers should not need to read the surrounding text to comprehend it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Think about what readers require to understand your text. Give each figure and table a number and an informative title (use sentence case). Use software packages to make figures and tables look professional.

rubrics_metrics.name: Figure and table numbering (chapter-specific)
rubrics_metrics.description: Figure numbering should be chapter specific, so figures in the introduction are numbered 1.1, 1.2, 1.3 etc. Tables should be numbered independently but taking a similar approach (e.g. 1.1, 1.2...).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure consistency in numbering across chapters and between figures and tables.

rubrics_metrics.name: Referencing figures and tables in text
rubrics_metrics.description: All figures and tables must be referred to in the text before they appear.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid abbreviations in figures/tables
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid abbreviations in figures and tables where possible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If you need to use an abbreviation, provide a key in the figure/table itself.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choosing between graphs and text
rubrics_metrics.description: Decide whether the data is best communicated through a figure: if there is one curve on a graph, could you describe it in sentences to better effect?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a figure/table is necessary, decide which type of illustration is appropriate: show exact numerical values (table) or trend/pattern (graph).

rubrics_metrics.name: Graphs — axis labels and independent/dependent variables
rubrics_metrics.description: Label the axes on each graph accurately and fully: what is being plotted and what are the units? In graphs always plot the independent variable on the X axis (and the dependent variable on the Y axis).

rubrics_metrics.name: Graphs — avoid overcrowding and ensure distinguishability
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid presenting overcrowded graphs; sometimes it is better to have two graphs rather than one that is congested.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure that each line on your graph is easily distinguishable from the others.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tables — when to use and content
rubrics_metrics.description: Tables should be used when repetitive data need to be presented. Think carefully whether the information could be presented in the text rather than in a table.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When presenting numbers, provide significant figures only. Do not include non-essential data such as results of simple calculations. Do not present the same data in the text that you provide in a table (avoid needless repetition).

rubrics_metrics.name: Table layout and presentation
rubrics_metrics.description: Decide whether it is best to present information horizontally or vertically. Numbers in a column are lined up on the right; words in a column are lined up on the left.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide headings that make the meaning of the data clear. If necessary provide short, precise explanatory footnotes. Provide a concise, precise title for the table; omit unnecessary words.

rubrics_metrics.name: Numbers and numerals — basic conventions
rubrics_metrics.description: Numbers one to nine should be written in full (e.g. one, two, three). Numerals should be used to express numbers 10 and larger (e.g. 200, 550). In a graphical display, numerals should always be used.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Numerals are used to express numbers below 10 that are grouped with numbers 10 and larger (e.g. 8 of 32 test cases). Numerals are used preceding units of measurement, for mathematical/statistical data, fractions, decimals, ratios and percentages, dates/times/ages/sample sizes, page numbers, and parts of tables/figures. If a sentence begins with a number, write it in full or rewrite the sentence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Numerals for measured quantities and mixed series
rubrics_metrics.description: Use numerals for measured quantities (weights, distances, decimal points) and for mixed series of numbers greater than and less than ten.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow the conventions summarized in Table 7.1: counts one-to-nine use words, counts 10+ use numerals, percentages use numerals, fractions use words, dates/times use numerals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clarity and simplicity in scientific writing
rubrics_metrics.description: Clarity is the key feature of scientific writing; use a simple, precise style and do not try to write elaborate sentences to impress readers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A thesis contributes new knowledge; absolute clarity is required. Consult specialist texts for models and check discipline-specific style differences with your supervisor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sentences and vocabulary
rubrics_metrics.description: Use short, clear, declarative sentences; mix up sentence length to avoid monotony. Use linking words (e.g. moreover, additionally) to show argument development; use contrast words (e.g. however) to link disagreeing clauses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Place a full stop or semi-colon before linking words when connecting two independent clauses (do not use a comma splice). Be precise with word choice (do not use 'while' if you mean 'although', or 'since' if you mean 'because'). Keep consistent terminology — use the same word for the same thing throughout.

rubrics_metrics.name: Paragraphing — structure and length
rubrics_metrics.description: A paragraph should make one point. Aim for a paragraph length between 100 and 200 words (roughly a third to two-thirds of a page double-spaced).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Organize paragraphs as Topic → Main Body → Wrap up. The first sentence (topic sentence) introduces the paragraph's focus; the wrap-up gives a mini-conclusion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Verb tenses
rubrics_metrics.description: Use the simple past tense when stating what has been done (e.g. 'The injection was administered'). Use the present tense for statements of fact (e.g. 'Developmental biology is the study of the growth of an organism').

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid double negatives
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not use double negatives; instead, write affirmative sentences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Table 8.1 gives examples converting double negatives into affirmative forms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Placement of 'only'
rubrics_metrics.description: Be careful when using 'only' — its meaning changes depending on placement in the sentence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples show different meanings depending on placement (e.g. 'Only the smallest group was injected' vs 'The smallest group was only injected'). Ensure placement matches intended meaning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of 'to comprise'
rubrics_metrics.description: 'To comprise' means 'to consist of' or 'to contain'. It should not be used instead of 'to compose'. Do not write 'is comprised of': it is incorrect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Correct: 'A thesis comprises several chapters.' Incorrect: 'A thesis is comprised of several chapters.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Abbreviations — introduction and avoidance
rubrics_metrics.description: In general, avoid abbreviations except for standard units of measurement and their SI prefixes. If you use an abbreviation, introduce it by writing the term in full first followed by the abbreviation in parentheses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Abbreviate units of measurement when used with numerical measurement (e.g. '6 mg'). Do not start sentences with an abbreviation. Refer to section 6.4.6 for more info.

rubrics_metrics.name: Commonly confused words — usage rules
rubrics_metrics.description: Use the correct form for commonly confused words: there/their/they're; this/that; greater than/more than vs 'in excess of'; fewer/less; among/between; assure/ensure/insure; affect/effect/impact; with/to in comparisons, etc.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The manual provides tables and examples showing correct/incorrect usages and guidance on ambiguity (e.g. prefer 'greater than' to 'in excess of'; use 'fewer' for countable, 'less' for quantity).

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid jargon, slang and wordiness
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid using jargon and slang in academic writing; use precise, accurate words and expressions instead. Wordiness obscures meaning and irritates readers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The guide lists jargon/slang phrases and wordy phrases to avoid. In methods and results be specific rather than general (e.g. 'Data were analysed by two-way ANOVA followed by Tukey’s post-hoc test' rather than 'Statistical analyses were carried out'). Use single words instead of phrases where possible (see tables of succinct alternatives).

rubrics_metrics.name: Contractions — avoid
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not use contractions in academic writing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Replace 'Isn’t' with 'Is not', 'Couldn’t' with 'Could not', 'It’s' with 'It is', etc.

rubrics_metrics.name: Gender‑neutral language
rubrics_metrics.description: Use terms that do not emphasize outdated gender roles; aim to write in an unbiased, gender-neutral style and be consistent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use 'humans' or 'people' instead of 'man'; use 'they' and 'their' instead of 'he' and 'his' where appropriate; see provided tables of outdated/gender-neutral equivalents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Grammar — comparisons, commas, encapsulating, prepositions, pronouns
rubrics_metrics.description: Follow rules for comparisons (avoid double comparatives), correct comma usage to avoid changing meaning, avoid encapsulating ambiguity (single word referring to previous idea incorrectly), avoid ending sentences with prepositions, and ensure pronoun-verb agreement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples illustrate errors and corrections (e.g., 'Patient A’s bruising was darker than Patient B’s'; 'Each of the laws was passed...'). Connecting words should not be used to begin sentences when they join clauses improperly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid common punctuation/structural errors
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not use exclamation marks in academic writing. Avoid overuse of parentheses. Do not use a comma to join two independent clauses (comma splice).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Replace exclamation marks with full stops; consider whether parenthetical information is necessary; use a full stop, semi-colon or colon to join independent clauses instead of a comma.

rubrics_metrics.name: Punctuation — specific rules and uses
rubrics_metrics.description: Follow punctuation rules: apostrophe for possession (and not for its), square brackets for words added in quotations, round brackets for illustrative info, capitalization rules, use of colon to introduce lists/quotations/strong statements, comma uses (lists, separating parts, subordinate clauses, adverbs at sentence start), dash for asides, ellipsis for missing words, quotation mark conventions, semi-colon to separate independent clauses or complex list items.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The guide gives detailed examples for each mark (e.g. table of punctuation, examples of colon and semi-colon usage). Learn from published work in your discipline and consult specialist guides if needed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Spelling vigilance and specialist terms
rubrics_metrics.description: Use spellcheckers but be vigilant for specialist/technical terms which may not be recognized. Learn correct spelling of key discipline terms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: You may add technical words to the spellchecker dictionary but ensure correct spelling. Create a glossary of specialist words to assist your writing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proofreading — use checklists
rubrics_metrics.description: Use proofreading checklists to catch punctuation, grammar, spelling and formatting errors before submission.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep a log of mistakes you make and form a habit of consulting reference works and electronic grammar checkers; focus on correcting recurring errors.
